dailyBrief.text: Good morning, Smileys — it's homecoming day: Benji is expected to be discharged today, with his first pediatrician appointment already booked for tomorrow, and Solon is giving you a beautiful day for it, mostly sunny with a high near 73°. It is also Election Day: Ohio polls are open 6:30 AM to 7:30 PM, the governor's race between Amy Acton and Vivek Ramaswamy and the Senate race between Jon Husted and Sherrod Brown are both close, and 66 Cuyahoga County precincts — including some in Solon — have new polling places, so check yours before you go. Overnight the U.S. carried out limited strikes on Iranian missile targets on Qeshm Island while talks remained possible, and the Cavs lost a close one to Oklahoma City, 117-112, despite the game staying tight into the final minute. Tonight, after the ride home and a first evening as a family of four (plus Moose), the results start rolling in after Ohio polls close at 7:30.

items.title: Cavs vs Oklahoma City Thunder
Russia pounds Ukraine's power grid in one of the war's biggest barrages, a week before peace talks resume
items.summary:
Russia launched one of the largest attacks of the war on Ukraine's energy system overnight, sending 289 drones, 17 ballistic missiles and 59 cruise missiles at power plants and substations from Odesa in the south to Rivne in the west. Power was cut across Kyiv and at least six other regions, water and transport in the capital were disrupted, and DTEK, Ukraine's largest private power company, said three of its five thermal plants were knocked offline.

In Dnipro, two people were killed and about 20 wounded, and a train station and passenger carriages were hit. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy also updated the toll from Monday's double strike on a school used as an aid centre in Komyshuvakha to at least 33 dead, with about 50 people still believed buried — Moscow says it targeted military units there.

Zelenskyy made the timing point himself in Berlin, standing beside Chancellor Friedrich Merz: the barrage landed on the day of the U.S. congressional elections, less than two days after a short humanitarian truce near Oleshky expired. Merz called the upcoming talks the right step but said he had seen no sign Russia was ready to negotiate seriously.

U.S.-brokered trilateral talks are set for Abu Dhabi on November 10-11, with European and NATO consultations in the days just before. Watch whether Ukraine heads into winter — and into those talks — with its grid repaired or still dark.

items.title: U.S. struck Iran's Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz in a limited strike kept deliberately quiet
items.summary:
The United States struck Iran's Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, according to a Wall Street Journal report cited by Reuters, with U.S. officials describing the action as limited and defensive. Iran's state media reported several explosions on the island, and one account said a missile launcher was hit after Iranian fire brought down a U.S. drone east of the strait.

The strike was the latest in a series of smaller actions in recent weeks that officials said were deliberately kept low-profile, so they would not read as a restart of the major military campaign. U.S. Central Command had issued no formal public statement as of Tuesday, and a U.S. official told Reuters the strikes did not mark a return to major combat.

The two tracks are running at once. The U.S. and Iran have been at war since late February, traffic through Hormuz — once about a fifth of the world's oil and gas — has fallen sharply, and yet President Trump said Monday that a deal could still happen and answered 'no' when asked if he was considering striking Iran after the midterms. Oil edged up about half a percent Tuesday, with Brent near $105 a barrel.

Watch what happens after Election Day. Tehran says contacts to end the war are continuing, so the next strikes — or the lack of them — will say more than the statements.

items.title: Trump says U.S. aid to Israel, about $4 billion a year, will be cut off at the end of the year
items.summary:
President Donald Trump said on Fox & Friends on Election Day that the United States will end roughly $4 billion a year in aid to Israel by the end of the year. He said he had reached an agreement with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, that the idea was Netanyahu's, and that the two had discussed it for a couple of years before settling it months ago.

'Israel's our number one recipient, we give them more than anybody else. And they no longer need it,' Trump said, calling Israel a thriving country and a great ally. He stressed that Israel could still buy American weapons — what ends is grant aid — and that Washington would still help if Israel needed it.

The standing agreement is actually $3.8 billion a year through fiscal 2028, so a cutoff at the end of 2026 would land about two years early, and it would compress into weeks the drawdown Netanyahu himself floated in May, when he spoke of bringing U.S. support to zero over ten years. Funding also runs through Congress, and as of Tuesday afternoon there had been no joint announcement and no public order spelling out which accounts end; reporting in Israel said neither the military nor the treasury there was aware of the decision.

Watch for a reaction from Netanyahu's office and from Congress, where aid to Israel was already one of the most contentious issues of the midterm campaign.

items.title: Hackers cranked supermarket freezers to 122 degrees across Europe — a second wave in three weeks
items.summary:
Supermarkets across Europe spent Tuesday rushing to patch and unplug their refrigeration systems after a second wave of cyberattacks tampered with fridges and freezers overnight Monday. Stores in eight countries were hit, food had to be thrown away in large quantities, and in one Swedish ICA store freezers were set to 50 degrees Celsius — about 122 Fahrenheit — with staff saying everything inside was destroyed.

The attack looked identical to one that swept dozens of French supermarkets three weeks ago. Carrefour, hit at 80 franchised stores in France in the first wave, was hit again at 15 stores in Belgium. Sweden's Coop chain is moving its systems onto 5G networks and has disconnected refrigeration at the seven stores hit, while the software provider Danfoss repeated its warning that refrigeration controllers should never be directly reachable from the internet.

No one has claimed responsibility, and investigators have not established who is behind either wave or whether they are linked. The EU cybersecurity agency ENISA said the multi-country scale underlines the need for rapid information-sharing, and Britain's cyber chief said his agency is on heightened alert after hackers probed small meat-processing firms there.

Watch whether U.S. chains using similar equipment take the same precaution. The uncomfortable lesson is how much of the food supply runs on internet-connected controllers that were never hardened like IT systems.

items.title: World Court will rule November 19 in the Rohingya genocide case against Myanmar
items.summary:
The International Court of Justice announced Tuesday that it will deliver its judgment on November 19 in the case accusing Myanmar of genocide against the Rohingya, its Muslim minority. Judges at The Hague will begin reading the ruling that morning, closing a case The Gambia brought in 2019.

The case centres on Myanmar's 2017 military offensive, which drove at least 730,000 Rohingya into neighbouring Bangladesh. Refugees described killings, mass rape and villages burned, and a United Nations fact-finding mission concluded the campaign included genocidal acts. Myanmar denies genocide and says the operation was a legitimate counter-terrorism campaign.

This will be only the third genocide judgment in the court's history, and the first in more than a decade. Genocide is rarely proven in international courts because judges must find the crimes were committed with the specific intent to destroy a group, in whole or in part — a deliberately high bar. The court's rulings are final, with no appeal.

The reach goes well beyond Myanmar. Whatever standard the judges set is expected to shape the other genocide case now before the court, South Africa's case accusing Israel over Gaza, which Israel denies.

items.title: Cyclone Murasu makes landfall on India's east coast, the second storm to hit in a week
items.summary:
Cyclone Murasu began coming ashore on India's eastern coast in the early hours of Tuesday, making landfall around 1 a.m. local time in Andhra Pradesh, according to the India Meteorological Department. Authorities had spent Monday moving people out of its path and planned to evacuate roughly 30,000 residents.

Murasu formed over the Bay of Bengal, the body of water that has produced some of the deadliest storms in the region's history. Forecasters expected Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu, its southern neighbour, to take the worst of the wind and rain.

It is the second storm to hit the same coastline in a week. The previous one, Cyclone Arnab, came ashore in Andhra Pradesh last Wednesday and killed at least six people, so emergency crews and shelters were already stretched before Murasu arrived.

Damage and casualty figures for Murasu itself had not been reported as the storm came ashore. Watch the daylight assessments — back-to-back landfalls on the same stretch of coast are what turn a severe storm into a prolonged relief problem.

items.title: Early voter poll finds an angry electorate: most disapprove of Trump, and cost of living drove the vote
items.summary:
The first findings from CNN's Voter Poll — the large survey of roughly 100,000 voters that has succeeded the traditional exit poll — paint a bleak national mood. About three-quarters of voters say they are dissatisfied or worse with how things are going in the country, and around four in ten describe themselves as angry.

About six in ten voters disapprove of President Donald Trump's job performance, roughly half of them strongly, and about a fifth of people who voted for Trump in 2024 now disapprove. Around three-quarters call economic conditions bad, about nine in ten say cost of living was crucial or a major factor in their vote, and roughly two-thirds say Trump has made economic conditions worse. The economy ranked as the top issue, ahead of the state of democracy, with immigration, healthcare, foreign policy and crime well behind.

Fewer than a fifth of voters said their House vote was cast in support of Trump; the rest said they were voting against him or that he was not a factor. Most voters also said the administration has gone too far on immigration enforcement and that the U.S. made the wrong decision taking military action against Iran, according to the early findings.

CNN stresses these are preliminary estimates, not results — the numbers have not yet been adjusted to match the actual outcome. Watch how closely tonight's results track this mood, especially in the Senate races.

items.title: North Carolina extends voting at five precincts, pushing its first statewide results to about 8:15 p.m.
items.summary:
North Carolina's State Board of Elections voted Tuesday to keep voting open later at five precincts in four counties where voting was interrupted during the day. Because state law bars releasing any unofficial results while voting continues anywhere in a contest, the decision delays the state's first results until about 8:15 p.m.

The longest extension is in Columbus County, where computer problems delayed one precinct's opening by nearly an hour and affidavits indicated 15 to 30 people left without voting; it will stay open until 8:15 p.m. Two Hertford County sites were extended to 7:55 and 8:00 p.m., a Lenoir County site where printers were down for about 45 minutes to 8:00 p.m., and a Wilson County site to 7:45 p.m.

State law only allows an extension where voting stopped for at least 15 minutes, and only for as long as the disruption lasted. Anyone voting after the normal 7:30 p.m. close at those sites will cast a provisional ballot.

North Carolina has about 2,625 polling places, and officials note brief disruptions are routine. But on a night when control of the Senate may hinge on a handful of states, even a 45-minute delay in one state's first numbers is worth knowing about.
items.source: North Carolina State Board of Elections

items.title: Floods force Florida polling places to move on Election Day, with 200-plus water rescues in Brevard County
items.summary:
Election Day in Brevard County, Florida, arrived in the middle of a flood emergency. More than 17 inches of rain fell around Melbourne in 24 hours, over 23 inches in Grant-Valkaria, and parts of southern Brevard topped 20 inches — an event the sheriff dubbed the 'November Rain Storm of '26.'

The sheriff's office reported 2,100 calls for service since Monday morning and 204 high-water rescues, with boil-water notices still in effect in Melbourne and Palm Bay on Tuesday morning and many roads still closed. The county's elections supervisor said six polling locations had to be relocated because the sites were completely unusable — flooded, damaged, or without power. Voters who could not reach their polling place could get an emergency mail ballot at one of four elections offices.

Governor Ron DeSantis declared an emergency over the flooding, and the state's elections division listed relocated polling places in seven more counties, including Broward and Palm Beach. In Palm Beach County, some voters in flooded neighbourhoods reached the polls by kayak and paddle board.

Many poll workers showed up despite their own homes flooding. Watch the county's turnout and any challenges tonight — when a polling place moves on Election Day itself, some voters inevitably go to the old address first.

items.title: South Carolina breaks its gubernatorial-election turnout record before the polls even close
items.summary:
By 4:30 p.m. Tuesday, 1,797,335 South Carolinians had cast ballots — 52.3% of registered voters — already surpassing the state's previous record total for a gubernatorial election, set in 2018, with more than two hours of voting still to go. The State Election Commission called it the highest total in a gubernatorial election in 30 years.

The number also passed the entire 2022 midterm total of just over 1.7 million. More than 421,000 of Tuesday's ballots were cast on Election Day itself by noon, on top of more than a million early ballots — roughly double the early vote of 2022. The state's all-time turnout percentage record, 54.6% from 2002, was within reach by the 7 p.m. close.

What is pulling people out is a full slate: the governor's office, every U.S. House seat, the state House, and a U.S. Senate race that was described as deadlocked in its final days — a seat long considered safely Republican that has become a genuine toss-up.

Turnout is not a result, and a record electorate does not by itself say who wins. But when a state breaks its midterm record before dinner, both parties will claim the new voters are theirs — tonight's returns will settle that argument.

items.title: Michigan Democrat who endorsed the Republican for Senate seeks marshals' protection after death threats, Axios reports
items.summary:
Representative Haley Stevens of Michigan has asked the U.S. Marshals Service for protection after receiving death threats for endorsing Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan's Senate race, Axios reported Tuesday afternoon, citing two senior Trump administration officials. The report, carried in live election coverage, has not been independently confirmed.

Stevens lost the Democratic Senate primary to Abdul El-Sayed, then endorsed Rogers on Sunday after appearing with him at a church service. The cross-party endorsement drew wide criticism from Democrats, and her top staff members resigned. El-Sayed's campaign said it raised $1.2 million in the four hours after the endorsement was announced.

Michigan's race between Rogers and El-Sayed is one of the most closely watched of the midterms. Democrats need a net gain of four seats to flip the Senate; a 50-50 chamber stays Republican on Vice President JD Vance's tie-breaking vote. El-Sayed told reporters Tuesday, after visiting a polling place, that he was bracing for possible challenges to the results.

Michigan polls close at 8 p.m. Eastern. Watch both the count and the reaction to it — this race now carries a personal-safety story on top of its national stakes.

items.title: Alaska's 'Decoy Dan' is missing on Election Day, and Trump calls the same-name candidacy a criminal act
items.summary:
One of the strangest races of the midterms got stranger on Election Day: Daniel J. Sullivan, the independent Alaska Senate candidate who shares a name with incumbent Republican Senator Daniel S. Sullivan, held no events, did not answer calls or messages, and by all accounts remained missing from the campaign trail.

Sullivan left the town of Petersburg last Monday; a former student reported spotting him on a flight to Anchorage. His voicemail, reached Tuesday, played a Halloween-themed message. In Alaska's August jungle primary he took 2.5% of the vote — small, but in a state that uses ranked-choice voting and where the polling average has Democrat Mary Peltola about a point ahead of the incumbent, a same-name candidate on the ballot is a real source of confusion.

President Trump weighed in on Fox & Friends on Tuesday morning, calling the candidacy 'a total fraud' and 'a criminal act.' The Justice Department opened a probe, and a lawsuit seeking to block certification if the incumbent loses was dismissed by a federal judge on November 1, though the department is appealing, according to other coverage. Peltola's campaign has denied allegations, reported by The New York Times, that it recruited the namesake candidate.

The incumbent was reduced on Election Day to urging voters to 'vote for the right Dan Sullivan.' With ranked-choice tabulation, Alaska's answer may take days — and the namesake question may outlast the count.

items.title: Markets close split on Election Day: chips lift the S&P and Nasdaq while Apple drags the Dow lower
items.summary:
Wall Street finished Election Day pointing in two directions. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 0.38% to 51,786.72, while the S&P 500 rose 0.36% to 7,568.92 and the Nasdaq Composite gained 0.83% to 25,372.01. The small-cap Russell 2000 added 0.23%.

The split had a simple cause. Apple fell about 1.9% after its weaker margin outlook and disappointing iPad sales the night before, and because the Dow is weighted by share price, Apple's slide pulled that index into the red on its own. Chip stocks did the opposite work for the broader market: Nvidia rebounded and semiconductor shares jumped after Monday's AI selloff, which had pushed the Nasdaq-100 into correction territory.

Oil went the other way from stocks' optimism about diplomacy — Brent crude eased to about $103.60 a barrel in the close wrap, extending Monday's near-8% plunge on hopes of U.S.-Iran talks, even as news of the Qeshm Island strike circulated.

Investors were also pricing the election itself, with prediction markets leaning toward a strong Democratic night. One bank warning making the rounds: a Democratic sweep could trigger weakness in AI-related stocks. Tonight's results will test both the politics and the chip rebound.

items.title: AMD posts a record quarter: revenue up 45%, data centre sales nearly double, and a $17 billion guide
items.summary:
AMD reported third-quarter results after the close that beat expectations across its most important lines. Revenue rose 45% to $13.38 billion, ahead of estimates near $13.1 billion, and adjusted earnings of $2.09 a share topped the $1.95 analysts expected.

The engine was the data centre. That segment's revenue jumped 97% to a record $8.55 billion, beating estimates of $8.2 billion, on demand for Instinct AI accelerators and EPYC server processors as AI workloads shift toward real-world inference. AMD's flagship Helios rack, combining its MI455X accelerator with new 'Venice' server chips, is in production and being tested at Meta, which agreed in February to buy up to $60 billion of AMD chips over five years.

Guidance did the rest: AMD forecast about $17 billion in fourth-quarter revenue, above the roughly $16.3 billion analysts expected, and shares rose more than 6% in extended trading. The soft spot was Client and Gaming, down 8%, with gaming revenue falling about 40%.

AMD is taking share from Intel while a global shortage of high-bandwidth memory squeezes the whole industry. Watch whether the Q4 ramp of Helios systems holds — that delivery schedule is now the stock's story.

items.title: Super Micro blows past estimates on AI server demand and raises its full-year outlook by billions
items.summary:
Super Micro Computer reported fiscal first-quarter revenue of $19.95 billion, far above the $16.39 billion analysts had expected, as cloud providers and tech companies keep expanding data-centre capacity. Adjusted earnings of $1.81 a share also cleared the $1.23 estimate comfortably, and gross margin of 12.7% came in ahead of the company's own preliminary range.

The outlook was bigger still. Super Micro forecast second-quarter revenue of $19.5 to $21.5 billion, against a Street estimate near $17.1 billion, and raised its fiscal 2027 revenue forecast to $72 to $82 billion, up from $65 to $72 billion and above the roughly $69 billion analysts expected.

The San Jose company is one of the purest beneficiaries of the AI buildout, selling Nvidia-powered systems into the data-centre boom. Its results land alongside AMD's record quarter and Arista's networking surge as evidence that AI infrastructure spending is still accelerating into 2027.

Two cautions sit behind the numbers: the company only last month appointed a new CFO after a nearly two-year search amid accounting concerns, and a contractor pleaded guilty last month in a case involving illegal exports of servers with advanced Nvidia chips to China. Watch whether the raised forecast survives those governance questions.

items.title: Arista Networks grows revenue 58%, its fastest since its IPO, as AI data centres buy networking gear
items.summary:
Arista Networks reported third-quarter revenue of $3.66 billion, up 58.5% from a year earlier — its fastest growth since its 2014 initial public offering — and well above both analyst estimates near $3.34 billion and its own $3.3 billion guidance. Adjusted earnings rose 60% to $1.20 a share, beating the $1.08 expected.

Arista sells the high-speed Ethernet networking that connects clusters of servers inside cloud data centres, and AI has turned that back-end gear into a bottleneck worth spending on. Its biggest customers are Microsoft and Meta, with Oracle and Google newer additions to the list, and the company has forecast at least $3.5 billion of AI-related revenue in 2026.

Fourth-quarter guidance of $3.9 to $4.0 billion also came in well above estimates around $3.6 billion. The stock climbed more than 15% in extended trading, recovering ground lost since its October high.

The competitive question is share: Arista faces Cisco and HPE's Juniper unit, plus pressure from contract manufacturers building similar switches. For now, its numbers say the AI buildout's plumbing is growing as fast as the chips it connects.

items.title: Block raises its full-year outlook as Cash App gross profit jumps 27%
items.summary:
Block, the payments company led by Jack Dorsey, raised its full-year outlook after a third quarter powered by Cash App. Cash App's gross profit surged 27% from a year earlier, the Square merchant business grew gross profit 14%, and adjusted operating income rose to $923 million, or $1.13 a share, up from $480 million a year earlier.

Cash App reached 60 million monthly transacting users in September, growth Dorsey credited in his shareholder letter to its 'Neighborhoods' feature. Management said Cash App Card spending and repayment rates on its Borrow product suggest consumers are managing their finances, even against an uncertain economic backdrop.

Block now expects 2026 gross profit of $12.63 billion, up from $12.51 billion, implying 22% growth, and gave an initial 2027 figure of $14.52 billion. Executives also said the fourth quarter should be the first in which Block earns revenue directly from AI tools.

One number to watch: losses on transaction, loan and consumer receivables rose about 66% to $601.7 million in the quarter, as lending becomes a bigger part of the business. The stock slipped modestly after hours despite the raise, per Wall Street Journal coverage.

items.title: Election Day storm soaks the central U.S. after deadly, historic flooding in the Southwest
items.summary:
The storm system that produced deadly, historic flooding in the Southwest over the weekend spread widespread rain across the central United States on Election Day, stretching from the Great Plains and Upper Midwest through the Mississippi Valley to the western Gulf Coast. In the Southwest it dropped several months' worth of rain, pushed rivers and washes past major flood stage — some to record highs in Arizona and Colorado — and forced evacuations in at least a dozen counties across four states.

In Flagstaff, Arizona, a 73-year-old man was found dead Monday after reportedly falling into floodwater, and a second man was found dead in a stormwater drainage area. Arizona's governor declared a statewide emergency, and in Colorado the San Juan River at Pagosa Springs surged to its second-highest level on record, forcing evacuations and the relocation of a voting centre and ballot drop box.

Florida took its own hit from separate flooding: more than 20 inches of rain forced officials to move 23 polling places, and at least two deaths around Palm Bay were linked to the water.

A few storms turned severe Tuesday afternoon near the Louisiana-Texas border. The same system that rearranged Election Day logistics across three regions is a reminder of how much of this vote happened under emergency conditions.

items.title: Voting ran mostly smoothly nationwide, with scattered glitches: failed scanners, bomb threats and two-hour lines
items.summary:
For all the build-up, Election Day voting across the country was mostly uneventful, with no evidence of widespread problems by Tuesday afternoon, according to USA TODAY's reporting. About 50 million ballots had been cast early, and election officials in most places reported a normal, if busy, day.

The exceptions were specific. In Westchester County, New York, ballot scanners failed county-wide at the start of the day; officials first blamed ballot paper thickness, retracted that, and by afternoon traced the failure to an update to the county's election programming issued after equipment testing. Voters kept casting paper ballots into secure emergency bags for later counting, and New York's attorney general said her office was monitoring. In Toledo, Ohio, a polling place at Beverly Elementary School received two bomb threats, pausing voting until a police sweep cleared the building.

Elsewhere, some lines in Tarrant County, Texas, topped two hours, isolated complaints surfaced about touchscreen machines in Tennessee, and flooding forced polling-place moves across Florida and parts of the Southwest.

Notably, by Tuesday afternoon there were no reports of armed federal officials at polling places, and the Department of Homeland Security said immigration agents were not planning operations at voting sites. The glitch list matters mainly where races are close enough for a precinct-level problem to become a legal one.

items.title: Oklahoma City man accused of mailing white-powder letters to election offices nationwide; case unsealed on Election Day
items.summary:
Federal prosecutors unsealed charges on Election Day against an Oklahoma City man accused of sending letters containing white powder to election offices across the country, as well as to members of Congress, media outlets, pollsters and the FBI. Robin Patrick Martin was arrested Monday and charged with conveying a hoax and mailing threatening communications.

An FBI agent's affidavit says investigators linked Martin to more than 700 mailings across the 2024 and 2026 election cycles from the same sender. The 2026 letters to election officials and party representatives carried a warning: 'CIVIL WAR IS COMING ON NOVEMBER 3RD!!' A 2024 mailing included a three-page letter titled 'DECLARATION OF WAR' and a warning that 'it won't be flour next time.'

One letter reached the Oklahoma State Election Board at the State Capitol on October 13; the office was evacuated after the powder was found, and no staff were harmed. The envelope carried a UV-readable message on the back. Martin, 67, is registered to vote in Oklahoma and Texas and works as a registered nurse in Texas, according to records cited in the case.

The affidavit argues any recipient would reasonably fear anthrax exposure from an unknown white powder — which is precisely the disruption such mailings are designed to cause at election offices. The case was still developing Tuesday.

items.title: Third U.S. bird flu death since the virus spread to dairy cattle, in Washington's Yakima County
items.summary:
A resident of Yakima County, Washington, has died after contracting H5N1 bird flu following exposure to infected dairy cattle, local health officials said — the third U.S. death linked to the virus since it began spreading among livestock, and the first U.S. bird flu death of 2026. The person, who had underlying health conditions, was hospitalised and died Sunday; the name was not released.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention identified the virus as H5N1. Washington officials say there have been three human infections in Yakima County since the virus was found in the state's dairy cattle, and 33 local dairy herds had recently tested positive. The H5 strain first spread to dairy cows in 2024, and most U.S. human cases since then have been farm workers, with mostly mild illness; the CDC has recorded more than 70 human cases nationally since 2024.

The two earlier deaths were an elderly person in Louisiana in 2025 and a Washington resident that November from the rarer H5N5 strain.

Yakima's health officer stressed that the virus can cause serious illness, especially in people with existing health problems, while the risk to the general public remains low. Watch whether the case prompts any change in guidance for dairy workers, who remain the group actually exposed.

items.title: FDA gives emergency authorization for Merck's Bravecto to treat screwworm infestations in dogs
items.summary:
The Food and Drug Administration on Tuesday issued an Emergency Use Authorization for Merck's Bravecto chewable tablets to treat New World screwworm infestations in dogs and puppies, expanding the options veterinarians have against the parasite. The authorization went to Intervet, Merck's U.S. animal health unit.

The FDA said that, on the totality of the scientific evidence, it is reasonable to believe Bravecto may be effective against screwworm in dogs and that the known and potential benefits outweigh the known and potential risks when the drug is used as authorized. Bravecto, whose active ingredient is fluralaner, was already approved for flea and tick indications.

Most U.S. dogs remain at low risk, the agency said, because confirmed screwworm cases are limited to a restricted geographic area. Dogs that live in, travel to, or return from affected regions should be watched for visible maggots or foul-smelling wounds, the signs of infestation.

The drug stays prescription-only through a licensed veterinarian, and the FDA noted the drug class has been associated with neurological side effects such as tremors and seizures. The authorization lasts until it is revoked or the underlying emergency declaration ends — a sign regulators are treating screwworm as a live animal-health threat worth pre-positioning treatments for.

items.title: Ohio picks its next governor today: Acton vs. Ramaswamy in a $200 million race, too early to call
items.summary:
Ohio voters are choosing their next governor today in one of the most expensive races in the country, between Republican entrepreneur Vivek Ramaswamy and Democrat Amy Acton. The winner replaces Governor Mike DeWine, who is term-limited. Libertarian Don Kissick is also on the ballot, and as of late afternoon the Associated Press had the race too early to call, with polls open until 7:30 p.m.

Both candidates are first-time statewide contenders with sharply different profiles. Acton, who announced in January 2025 and faced no Democratic primary, is the former state health director who became the face of Ohio's pandemic response. Ramaswamy launched in February 2025 with President Trump's endorsement. Candidates and their allies spent more than $200 million, according to AdImpact.

The final weeks turned personal — a Ramaswamy ad featuring Acton's estranged mother drew national attention — while the substantive fight ran over data centres, property taxes, affordability and Acton's pandemic record. Republican lawmakers also passed two Ramaswamy-backed measures, a 90-day gas tax suspension and a constitutional voter ID amendment that appears on today's ballot as Issue 3.

Absentee ballots must be in county board of elections hands by 7:30 p.m. to count. Ohio has not elected a Democratic governor in decades of trying — tonight says whether Acton's polling lead survives contact with Election Day turnout.

items.title: Record early turnout, and the three Cs — Cincinnati, Columbus and Cleveland — will decide Ohio tonight
items.summary:
Ohio set a new midterm record for in-person early voting before Election Day even arrived, with more than 1.7 million ballots already cast and mail voting down from past cycles. In Cuyahoga County, early voting was described as unprecedented, with lines snaking through the Board of Elections office in downtown Cleveland and final-weekend waits of over an hour.

The return pattern sets up tonight's tension. About 48% of registered Democrats who were issued ballots had already voted, compared with about 32% of Republicans — and Republicans traditionally vote in bigger numbers on Election Day itself. That makes the evening turnout in Cincinnati, Columbus and Cleveland the number to watch: Democrats need a big Cleveland showing, particularly from Black voters, in a county whose total turnout has slipped from 667,000 ballots in 2008 to 582,000 in 2024.

Two other counties will tell the state's story early. Mahoning County, Acton's hometown of Youngstown, flipped Republican in the Trump era, while Delaware County, Ohio's fastest-growing, has moved from a 35-point Republican win in 2000 to a 7-point one in 2024.

The Senate race layered on top — incumbent Republican Jon Husted against Democrat Sherrod Brown — is being called a nailbiter that could shape Senate control for the rest of Trump's presidency. Ohio's results start arriving after 7:30 p.m.

items.title: Justice Department sends 1,000 election monitors to all 50 states — including Cuyahoga County
items.summary:
The Justice Department released its Election Day list Tuesday: about 1,000 election monitors deployed across all 50 states, in what the department called the largest monitoring effort in its history. The effort is run by the Civil Rights Division, drawing on department staff, U.S. Attorney's offices and federal observers.

Ohio's share lands in three counties — Cuyahoga, Franklin and Medina. The department says monitors check compliance with federal voting-rights laws and stay in contact with state and local officials through the count, and it published a public complaint line for voting-rights concerns.

The deployment is drawing two opposite readings. The assistant attorney general for civil rights called election integrity one of the administration's top priorities. Voting-rights groups, including the NAACP, argue a large federal presence could suppress turnout and disenfranchise voters, particularly in minority communities — Cuyahoga County is about 30% Black, in a state that is about 13% Black overall.

The monitors arrive in a state deciding one of the hardest-fought Senate races in the country, between Jon Husted and Sherrod Brown. Watch for any incident reports out of the three Ohio counties tonight, and whether either campaign cites the federal presence in a challenge.

items.title: Ohio today is also JD Vance's first test toward 2028, a column argues
items.summary:
Vice President JD Vance closed the Ohio campaign with an Election Eve rally outside Toledo, capping weeks as a fixture in both of his home state's big races. A Columbus Dispatch / USA TODAY opinion column published Tuesday frames November 3 as something bigger than two races: Vance's first real test on the road to a possible 2028 presidential bid.

The logic is home-state arithmetic. The midterms are a referendum on President Trump's second term and, in part, on Vance himself — and no Republican has ever won the White House without carrying Ohio. A vice president who cannot deliver his own state hands future primary rivals a ready-made attack line. The Senate seat at stake is, pointedly, Vance's old seat, and it could decide control of the chamber.

Vance has not played it safe. When the Ramaswamy campaign's ad featuring Amy Acton's estranged mother drew criticism — including from Governor DeWine and Senator Husted, who said they would not have run it — Vance told Republicans to stop whining about it. Polling cited in the column put Brown slightly ahead of Husted and Acton ahead of Ramaswamy, with Trump's Ohio approval at 43% and the economy Ohio voters' top concern.

None of that makes tonight a Vance election. But if both Republicans lose in his home state, expect the 2028 conversation to start tomorrow morning, not in two years.

items.title: Rock & Roll Hall of Fame's $135 million expansion opens November 22, with its first dedicated indoor concert hall
items.summary:
The Rock & Roll Hall of Fame's $135 million expansion opens to the public on November 22, the museum announced, with a community day to mark it. The project adds 50,000 square feet west of the original I.M. Pei pyramid — the museum's largest construction project since its groundbreaking more than three decades ago.

The centrepiece is Baker Hall, an oval, two-floor room built for concerts and events — the museum's first indoor venue designed specifically for live music. Museum CEO Greg Harris said the ambition is plain: 'We want any artist that plays this to think this is the greatest room they've ever played in.' The new building also holds the Haslam Atrium, named for a $10 million gift from Browns owners Jimmy and Dee Haslam, and the entrance shifts into the new wing with a panoramic view of Lake Erie.

Outside, the Taylor Family Community Park will sit between the museum and the Great Lakes Science Center, operated by Cleveland Metroparks. The design is by New York firm Practice for Architecture and Urbanism, and about 95% of the money raised came from local donors.

Right after opening, work starts on redesigning the main exhibit hall, adding more than 10,000 square feet. And the induction ceremony returns to Cleveland in late 2027 — this year's is November 14 in Los Angeles.

items.title: Guardians closer Cade Smith is an AL Reliever of the Year finalist — as the Clase trial begins in Brooklyn
items.summary:
Cade Smith's first season as Cleveland's full-time closer has ended with national recognition: the 27-year-old is a finalist for American League Reliever of the Year, against Tampa Bay's Bryan Baker and Toronto's Louis Varland. Smith made 69 appearances, finished 60 games, posted a 1.95 ERA and led the majors with 41 saves, allowing only 16 earned runs while striking out 107.

He is not the only Guardian honoured. Rookie starter Parker Messick is a finalist for both AL Cy Young and AL Rookie of the Year, weeks after Cleveland's run to the American League Championship Series.

The timing carries an edge, because Smith got this job by succeeding Emmanuel Clase — the reliever of the year in 2022 and 2024, now out of the league. The same day Smith's finalist news was circulating, trial proceedings began in federal court in Brooklyn for Clase and Luis Ortiz, who face four counts including wire fraud conspiracy and conspiracy to influence sports contests by bribery, tied to alleged pitch-rigging for sports betting. Both have denied the allegations, and the charges carry up to 65 years in prison if they are convicted on all counts.

Cleveland's bullpen future looks settled either way. The trial will decide how the Clase era is remembered; Smith's season already decided who owns the ninth inning now.

baby.tip: Homecoming day tip: before you leave the hospital, do the car-seat check while help is still right there — base tight, straps snug at armpit level, and Benji's first ride home in a rear-facing seat in the back. Then tonight, keep it simple: one bag unpacked, feeding log started, and the diaper bag restocked for tomorrow's first pediatrician visit. If anything about feeding, breathing or temperature worries you at home, call the pediatrician or your OB team — that's exactly what they're there for.
baby.fact: Newborns sleep a lot but in short stretches — typically 16 to 17 hours a day, broken into naps of just a few hours at a time, because their tiny stomachs need frequent feeding. Benji's sleep will feel random this first week; short, frequent stretches around the clock are completely normal for a brand-new baby.
baby.fun: Today's tiny mission: the first family photo at home — Mike, Kelly, Benji and Moose in one frame (Moose at a calm, supervised distance for take one). It doesn't need to be perfect; the slightly chaotic version is the one you'll love most in a year.
